teachingPoints.text: Context pattern (pattern of dynamic properties) is illustrated as a common usage pattern.
A traversal function that walks a tree and performs an operation knows only how to traverse, so the concrete behaviour must be supplied from outside.
Separating traversal from the user operation keeps the walking code reusable across different behaviours.
The user operation is invoked per tree node and implements the strategy pattern, choosing how each node is processed.
A user operation may travel together with extra data such as a running current sum that starts at zero and grows as nodes are visited.
Because the per-node operation may accumulate context while traversing, a simple sum of node numbers is used as the running example.
A traversal operation can need the current node's depth level in addition to the node itself, which a plain delegate cannot always provide.
The operation may be more complex than a sum, for instance one that also depends on the depth level of the current node.
When the operation needs depth information it becomes an implementation of an interface rather than a plain function.
Such an interface exposes separate methods for entering a child node and for exiting back toward the parent, letting the operation track where it is in the traversal.
Giving the operation ordered enter and exit callbacks lets it maintain a correct depth counter without knowing the tree shape.
With a depth-aware strategy the numbers can be scaled by their depth, so the first level uses coefficient 1, the second 2, the third 3, producing 1, 2, 4, 6 for a run of ones.
The same logic can be implemented by incrementing a depth counter on the enter callback and decrementing it on the exit callback.
The depth counter itself must be kept in the shared context so it survives across node visits.
The proposed pattern is still not explained because the traversal function and the function that uses the strategy are bound together with it.
Even with depth tracking in the context this setup does not yet explain how the proposed pattern is meant to be used.
The traversal function and the strategy travel as a fixed pair, and the context is expected to be handed to the strategy from outside.
Because the strategy is invoked by the traversal function rather than by the external caller, the question becomes how an outside user can still pass a context into it.
The earlier workaround was to pass the strategy together with a link to its context as a single unit, so the running sum was a field of the strategy implementation class.
Now that the strategy is fixed to the traversal function, the context must be supplied when the whole grouping is created rather than through the strategy itself.
This leaves open the question of how to hand a context to that strategy.
To give the strategy a context, the context has to be supplied when the whole grouping of the traversal system and the strategy is created.
Attaching the context to the construction of the group is usually undesirable because doing so often requires global variables.
The global-variable workaround needs a mutex so the process runs once in one thread at a time, and all communication then happens through globals.
The goal is instead to let an external user pass context into the grouped system so it flows along with the node traversal.
One motivating example is a user who inspects the resulting context to print information about the data structure.
Another example is a strategy that mutates the nodes themselves, for example adding a value X to each node it visits.
Операция в примере может добавлять к каждой ноде число X, которое затем передаётся шагам пайплайна, чтобы шаги не были связаны с конкретной операцией.
В варианте, где X передаётся как параметр, операция не вызывает шаги сама, а лишь готовит данные для них.
Нельзя передать X напрямую операции, потому что она вызывается системой прохождения, а не пользователем, поэтому X должен приходить через общий контекст.
Пользователь контролирует стратегию, то есть выбор самих шагов, но сами шаги при этом не могут быть вызваны напрямую пользователем.
Стратегия применяется абстракцией, а не напрямую пользователем: абстракция взаимодействует со структурой данных, поэтому стратегия инкапсулирована.
Стратегии нужен внешний контекст для работы, потому что пользователь лишь передаёт его через систему прохождения.
Если слово контекст задано только снаружи, на нём нельзя строить несовместимые со свободным рынком рабочие места в коде.
Этот разбор показывает, что подходящим паттерном для такой задачи является паттерн стратегия.
Первый пример тот же пайплайн: функции вызываются друг за другом и передают друг другу контекст, то есть стратегия требует контекста для работы.
Пайплайн из предыдущих примеров устроен как последовательный вызов функций, передающих друг другу контекст.
Шаги пайплайна фиксированы и образуют стратегию, которая определяется при создании пайплайна.
В этом примере функция прохождения это цикл, который вызывает шаги по очереди, а сами шаги и есть стратегия.
Контекст передаётся между шагами циклом прохождения, чтобы после выполнения пайплайна можно было вывести полезную информацию.
В примере пайплайн искал число предыдущих владельцев, и это значение можно было вывести вместе с результатом работы пайплайна.
Суть примера: есть сами шаги и есть механизм прохождения по ним, они разделены.
Механизм прохождения не контролируется пользователем: его можно вызвать, но изменить его код пользователь не может.
Шаги пайплайна контролируются пользователем при создании пайплайна, а в рантайме пользователь выбирает только передаваемый контекст.
В рантайме пользователь выбирает контекст, который передаётся механизму прохождения, а не саму стратегию.
Определение стратегии совпадает с предыдущим: пользователь контролирует шаги, а система прохождения их применяет.
Стратегия фиксируется при создании, потому что шаги заданы списком в системе, и по этому списку можно проходить многократно.
Фиксированный список шагов позволяет вызвать прохождение много раз, и это типично для процессов с повторами.
Стратегия не применяется пользователем напрямую: пользователь передаёт контекст механизму прохождения, а тот вызывает шаги.
Стратегии необходим контекст, и именно механизм прохождения передаёт этот контекст между шагами.
Код прохода по шагам не должен знать содержимое контекста, иначе проход будет жёстко связан с текущей предметной областью.
Система прохождения не анализирует содержимое контекста, а лишь передаёт его шагам как есть.
Логика механизма прохождения не меняется в зависимости от того, какой контекст приходит на вход.
Система прохождения никак не интересуется данными контекста, поэтому контекст часто делают динамическим.
Динамический контекст собирается из сведений о произвольных сущностях, с которыми шаги ожидают работать в этом примере.
В игре существуют разные виды сущностей: например декоративная трава с позицией в мире, своим цветом и картинкой.
Другой вид сущности это вода со связанным шейдером, который рисует волны, и с параметрами вроде замедления игрока при попадании в воду.
У воды также может быть позиция в мире и физические свойства.
У игрока есть свои свойства: атака, скорость и здоровье.
В игре может быть система инвентаря, которая позволяет хранить предметы и использовать их.
A game entity carries plain data properties such as attack, speed and health, which is what makes it describable to systems later.
Игрок может быть системой инвентаря, которая позволяет ему хранить и применять предметы.
An entity may also reference supporting systems such as an inventory that lets it store and use items, and a zombie may get a simplified inventory with at least equipping.
Entities of different kinds can carry different data sets, e.g. an ordinary zombie with attack, health and speed versus a zombie that can use magic.
Because players, zombies, plants and other game elements differ only in which data they hold, all of them can be treated uniformly as entities.
There will be a container such as the game context that holds the data of all entities in the game, so systems have a single place to read state from.

One common entity type must be able to hold different kinds of data and combinations of them, from a mere position, sprite and color up to animations, stats, inventory items and what is currently held in hand.
Besides entity data there will be systems that operate on that data in the context.
Systems can be dedicated to a single concern, for example one that finds attack targets among enemies and one that applies enemy attacks to the chosen targets.
An inventory system can be a system that performs operations on inventory data that the user is currently trying to make.
Even gameplay rules like slowing the player down when they enter water must be implemented by some system, which shows how much of the game logic lives in systems.
The overall design is a set of independent pieces of functionality, each working with the game context.
Each system inspects entities in the context and expects the entities it interacts with to carry the required data.
A system either expects the data to be present or filters the entities down to only those that have it, so capabilities of entities drive which systems affect them.
A magic system therefore works only with entities that have the ability to use magic and ignores entities without it, such as bushes.
Such capability data is stored in the entity itself, alongside its other data in the same heap.
The user controls the strategy by choosing which data exists in which entities, so player intent enters the simulation through entity contents.
The user also controls which systems are enabled and which are disabled, which is the second half of the strategy.
The strategy is fixed at creation time because systems are built to work against the shared context and cannot be invoked for one particular entity.
Because of that, the strategy is applied by an abstraction rather than by the user directly, for example a magic system that searches all entities for the ones actually using magic and acts on them.
Systems need the context passed in from outside, which only works because entities themselves store the data the systems look for.
Entities are essentially the context through which the user influences the systems, so configuration lives in data rather than in direct system calls.
This example differs structurally from the pipeline example because the user's goal is a game simulation whose systems run autonomously to produce the player experience.
The goal is a simulation, so the systems must work autonomously and only need to deliver the intended experience to the player.
In the pipeline-style example the goal is instead to walk a list and pass each context onward through an abstraction, which changes how the same ideas read.
What does not change is the core idea that each entity holds properties an external system looks at; only the context in which that is applied differs.
The lesson moves on to a new project to illustrate the ideas in code, starting with the pipeline system where the context is supplied by the user including the context type.
In the pipeline design being introduced, the context is supplied by the user, including its type, so that execution can start from that context.
At this point in the lesson the context is still fixed, and the instructor notes that changing it will be covered later.
A pipeline step will be an interface whose single method receives the context as a parameter, so every step has one uniform entry point.
Each step receives the context so it can initialize itself, while the pipeline runs a fixed ordered sequence of those steps.
The pipeline is the abstraction that accepts the context from outside and passes it on to each of its steps.
A user calling Execute never passes the context to the steps directly; it flows through the pipeline abstraction instead.
Operations can live separately from the system or together with it, and in the combined case the explicit context is not needed at all.
To keep the example simple the context is temporarily removed, all of the structure is moved into a separate file, and only very simple handlers are created in the main file.
All of the structure is moved into its own file while the main file keeps only a few very simple handlers.
The handlers are a single simple step object that receives data and naturally exposes an Execute method.
Because Execute takes no context parameter, the only way to hand data to the step object is to pass it at construction time and store it in a field.
Usage becomes: instantiate the step, create the pipeline from it, and then execute the pipeline.
Running the program prints 'Hello, Антон', confirming that the step receives its data and the pipeline executes it.
The same system is used three times with the same data, and changing that data is not as easy as it looks because it is fixed at construction.
Storing the data inside the object this way behaves like global variables, since the step can be created once in advance and reused.
Because the data sits inside the constructed step, keeping it works like a global variable: the step is created once and reused.
The step can be created in advance with initial data 'Антон', and only after the whole structure is built can some data inside it be changed to another value such as 'собака' or 'кошка'.
The strategy object currently also carries the execution context, so changing the context means going inside the strategy and mutating its data.
The pipeline itself is meant to be fixed and immutable, that is, not to change after creation.
This usage mirrors global variables, so when the pipeline is used from two places, ideally from two threads, the pipeline itself should be immutable.
Because the pipeline is not immutable, it requires locks around that specific instance whenever it is used.
Since the pipeline is currently not immutable, using it from several threads forces locks around that particular pipeline instance.
Each thread must set the required context and then execute immediately, otherwise another thread could overwrite the context during the run.
If the context is not set and executed under one lock, another thread can overwrite it and the pipeline will end up executing the wrong work.
The price of this locking approach is resource contention: the other thread must block and wait until your execution finishes, which an immutable design would have avoided from the start.
The context should ideally be passed in fresh from outside on each Execute call rather than captured once when the pipeline is created.
This rule is not specific to pipelines but applies to any other abstraction following the same pattern, where the data arrives as a parameter of Execute.
The name should arrive as a parameter of Execute, but the caller constructs the pipeline itself so it cannot supply that value from outside, which is why a shared context object is needed.
Because the caller builds and runs the whole pipeline itself, there is no way to pass data into a particular step at pipeline invocation time.
A context object carrying the needed data must be created, passed as a parameter to Execute, and handed to every step so steps can read from it.
The context is named simply context and starts empty, so a name field is added to it to hold the value the greeting step needs.
Once name lives in the context, the step reads it from there, and each pipeline use can either create a fresh context or reuse one context and overwrite its data.
An alternative to creating a context per use is creating it once and reassigning the data inside it between runs.
The minimal form constructs the context inline in the call so no intermediate variable is needed, though the context class now also carries a field with the required data.
The step is bound to this specific context type and expects the required data to be present in it, so the context must expose a field with that data.
Hardcoding the greeting data in the context is bad because greeting the user is only one of several possible pipelines, and the same context would then have to serve unrelated data needs.
A second pipeline is sketched whose step adds a number to the context, which requires adding a sum field to the context alongside name.
The sum pipeline is built from two add steps (adding five and adding ten), added to the builder, and the resulting pipeline is executed with a context that initially holds nothing.
After passing the initially empty context into Execute, the demo prints the resulting id value to show what the run produced.
The demo notes this currently does not work, which sets up the explanation of why the shared context approach breaks down.
It does not work because the context was extended: the same object now carries data for the greeting pipeline and for the sum pipeline, mixing unrelated concerns in one context.
Mixing independent data in one bag is not inherently a problem, since unused fields can simply be initialized to something and left untouched by other pipelines.
One way to resolve this is to ignore the coupling and stuff every field the program might ever use into that single context structure.
This one-big-context approach is actually used in practice, especially in game programming.
This approach is named F-struct (Fract), and its advantage is that it is the simplest option and gives static, fully known usage of the data.
The drawback is that many of the fields go unused when a given pipeline uses the context, since different pipelines only need their own slice of the data.
A second drawback is that the context cannot be made part of an external system, because it has to know absolutely all information about how it will be used in the program.
The real problem appears when the pipeline builder and pipeline live in code you do not control: the context type is fixed there, so you cannot open its file and change its data or add fields to it.
The dynamic-properties pattern exists exactly for this case, letting a user attach their own data to a context type that was defined outside their code.
To pass data between pipeline steps the caller must first define the data in some form so it can be handed to the next stage.
A pipeline step can receive its data in several ways, and the valid options include an abstract base class, generics, or a dictionary/array-like component.
The lesson states the system offers many approaches to supplying such external context data and begins enumerating them with the first one.
The lesson focuses on the abstract-class approach, in which the context becomes abstract and all data is moved out of it.
After that change the pipeline step accepts any context that inherits from the abstract context class.
Technically you could pass a plain object instead, so the abstract context class is not the only possible mechanism.
The abstract context class prevents unexpected unrelated data from being passed into the pipeline step.
Having users explicitly inherit your context class documents intent and keeps the pipeline data flow more controlled.
The abstract context base is not strictly required for the pattern to work.
The code as it currently stands does not compile because a context is expected at that point.
Since the base context is abstract, every pipeline needs its own context class that inherits from it.
You also must create the type used by the math step and give it the necessary fields.
The context may hold other things too, such as a multiply-by-number value.
Additional steps working with the same context can exist, and the example adds one beyond the single minimal step.
Because the compiler cannot infer which type you mean, you must explicitly pass the concrete GreetingContext at every call site.
At run time the greeting pipeline expects that a context of exactly the required type arrives.
The context variable must therefore be cast to the concrete PrintContext the step expects.
The same explicit cast to the concrete math context type is required in the other step.
Every pipeline step that works with this context must cast, which is not ideal design.
The lesson defers explaining how to avoid these manual casts to a later discussion.
Since the math context inherits the abstract base, the cast is already redundant there and the code works unchanged.
The compiler cannot know that the pipeline accepts the greeting context specifically, only a generic context, so in principle you could even pass the math context here.
You could pass the math context where a greeting context is expected and the compiler would not treat it as an error.
At run time the cast to the greeting context fails, reporting that the math context cannot be cast to the greeting type the step expected.
This design trades a level of static type safety for extra flexibility, which is a very common pattern.
Generics partially solve this lost type safety and are covered later in the lesson.
The pattern also prevents building a mixed pipeline that both greets and multiplies within one flow.
You may still append the greeting step to this pipeline.
The compiler cannot enforce that a pipeline's steps all share one context type, so such mistakes surface only at run time.

A single pipeline cannot run a math step expecting a MathContext and a grid step expecting a GridContext together, because the two steps require different context types and the compiler rejects passing both through one abstraction.
Because the cast to GridContext happens inside the step, the mixed pipeline would fail at runtime rather than at the call site, which is why the breakage surfaces when the step actually runs.
Giving the two context types a common base class is the other way to get shared abstractions, but then you lose the ability to express mixed pipelines at all.
The game example frames the design: the system itself plays the role of the pipeline and the entities being processed play the role of the context passed through it.
Mixed pipelines that must run two independent operations against the same context at the same time occur often in real systems, so the restriction is not as exotic as it first appears.
In the tree example a second operation depends on a level value that only exists because the first operation stored it in the context, so the operations cannot be fully independent.
The concrete need is that each node result is multiplied by its own level value, so the same node variable is scaled by two, by three or by one depending on depth.
The level computation can be extracted into a separate strategy bundled with the main strategy in the same traversal, whose only job is to produce the level for the others.
Wrapping the main strategy with the decorator makes the level strategy run first, so it can compute and set the level before calling the wrapped strategy body.
Splitting the level computation into its own strategy is worthwhile because further strategies will need the very same level value.
A third strategy that also needs the level relies on the same decorator that sets the level, yet it lives in its own separate pipeline and box for the same traversal.
The same level-setting component is reused in both pipelines, which is what allows the other components around it to behave correctly in either place.
Even when the decorator does work unrelated to the main operation, the main operation may need context produced by that first operation, so the ordering has to be preserved.
Since walking the tree is expensive and should not be repeated, the traversal is done once with many strategies attached so they all execute for the same context.
In that design the strategies must be written into one traversal method as a long sequence of local variables, so the method grows with every added strategy.
The need for one traversal containing all strategies can be worked around by introducing interfaces that expose only what each step actually needs.
Adding a Get method for the name to the GridContext interface, implemented by returning the stored name or exposing it as a property, lets steps depend on a narrow contract.
The steps then cast to that interface rather than to the concrete context type, and an equivalent interface exposing the name property is declared for the math context.
Both steps only work if the passed context implements both interfaces, so an extra context type has to satisfy every interface the pipeline steps expect.
That extra class repeats all the data of the other contexts and is created and initialized at the call site so the mixed pipeline finally compiles.
The mixed pipeline now compiles only because that additional combined context type was introduced, which is the cost of the interface-based workaround.
After creating and initializing the missing object at this spot, the previously failing code now compiles, showing the missing declaration was the only obstacle.
The code compiles only because the steps were reworked to depend on context interfaces instead of concrete context classes, while the pipeline execution logic itself stayed unchanged.
Depending on an interface rather than a concrete class is a common and fully valid design, which motivates the next refactoring step.
Generics improve this by letting the builder declare at construction time which context type it is built for, instead of hard-coding a concrete context.
Because the builder is parameterized by a context type, the pipeline call on that builder will statically require exactly that context type.
Passing a different context type to such a builder is detected statically and reported as a compile error instead of failing later at runtime.
Adding a GridContext step to a pipeline that was typed with MathContext fails to compile, because the step's expected context type and the pipeline's context type disagree.
To make this work generically the concrete context type can be removed from the pipeline code and replaced by a type parameter, so the demonstration begins by erasing the concrete context.
The concrete context type is replaced by a generic parameter T standing for the context type, and that TContext is passed into the rest of the code.
PipelineBuilder and the pipeline itself must also depend on T, so the pipeline method accepts a TContext and stays type-consistent with the builder.
Those few changes are all the library needs to support any context type while still statically typing it.
The code does not compile at this intermediate stage because the builder has no way yet to declare which concrete context type each step expects.
Declaring the context type at builder creation makes each step parameter typed correctly, for example GridStep taking a GridContext, so no casts are required when adding steps.
This is what generics buy: a step added to the pipeline is guaranteed to receive the context type it expects.
A step that statically declares its context type will work with that type in any pipeline, and it is impossible to add it to a pipeline built for a different context type.
After introducing a MathContext class the code compiles, confirming the generic pipeline itself is type-correct.
The concrete steps still must be updated to work with MathContext, and the common ITypeContext abstraction can be deleted.
A generic interface is barely useful here because the generic argument must already name a concrete context type, so type mistakes are just as hard to make as with plain classes.
Two errors remain, and GridStep fails to compile because the pipeline now uses MathContext while GridStep expects a GridContext.
Once the pipeline is built for GridContext, adding the MathContext-typed steps errors, because each step statically demands the context type it expects and GridContext is not MathContext.
The offending call is commented out so the remaining compile errors can be inspected.
Passing a GridMaskContext into a pipeline that accepts MathContext will not compile, so the exact expected context type must be passed instead.
Generics keep the same flexibility as the previous abstract-class-and-subclass design but add static typing when the context is passed and when steps are added.
For this pipeline context the generic solution is complete at this point in the lesson.
Even if the grid step declared GridMaskContext as its context type, errors would remain because the number step expects MathContext while only GridContext is mentioned in the pipeline.
Instead of typing the pipeline step parameter with the concrete GdContext type, the step should depend on a generic context type parameter, which is what lets the same step work with any context.
The context type parameter is renamed everywhere from GdContext/MustContext to a neutral Context, so the step no longer names a specific context implementation.
Renaming the parameter to a generic context is still not enough on its own, because the compiler cannot verify that the runtime context implements the interface the step requires.
The compiler could infer the call since GdContext implements the context interface, but it needs an explicit hint at the call site before it will accept the step invocation.
Marking the pipeline step interface parameter with the input-only attribute, which declares that the context flows into the step but never back out, removes the compiler error.
This input-only declaration works only because the context arrives as a parameter of the interface implementation and is never returned, so nothing downstream depends on its concrete type.
The input-only parameter mechanism is named by C#'s covariance and contravariance rules, which the lesson points to as further reading.
The input-only parameter mechanism is named by C#'s covariance and contravariance rules, which the lesson points to as further reading.
This pattern is an example of contravariance: the supplied context type must implement at least the interface declared on the parameter, and may be a more derived type.
The grid step needs the same treatment, taking an ID step typed as a context interface rather than a GdContext.
After the change the code no longer compiles because the step now expects a context interface while the caller still supplies a grid-markup context.
Once the caller passes a matching context, compilation succeeds and the previously failing step call works.
Declaring the context as an interface keeps static typing while preserving flexibility, so two unrelated steps working with different context implementations can run in one pipeline.
A second approach called dynamic context exists alongside this one, and the lesson notes that so far all context has been static.
Because the builder is built around a concrete context type fixed at compile time, reading data out of the context previously required casting it to the expected type.
Whether a piece of data is present in the context, and what type it has, always depends statically on the declared context type, which limits what one context can carry.
A different approach lets you store varied data inside the same context type instead of being limited to the fields of one static context class.
The lesson creates a new plain Context class to hold the dynamic data; while it is empty nothing compiles against it.
All references are switched to the new Context type and the generic context parameters are removed from the step signatures.
The remaining generics and the old concrete context types are deleted everywhere so the pipeline only knows the single Context type.
Now nothing compiles, because the fields such as name and sum no longer exist on the context and cannot be initialized through it.
Dynamic context works by putting data into the context under some key and later taking it back out by the same key, so the context no longer needs statically declared fields.
In the example the caller stores the name under key zero and the sum under key one, so both values live in the same context.
One step reads the name back by key zero while another reads the sum by key one, showing that independent steps can consume different values from a single shared context.
The context therefore needs a way to write and read values by key, where the key could be an array position, a dictionary key, or a search over stored objects.
An array of objects is chosen as the underlying storage, and it must always be initialized from outside the context before the steps run.
The step declares public constants Name = 0 and One = 1 that name array positions, so callers and the step share one agreed layout.
The constants can be used inside the step because they mark the expected positions of the data the step needs from the context array.
The step reads the context data array at the index given by the key constant and treats the retrieved value as a string.
The retrieved element arrives as object, so it is cast to string because the step prints it and printing works with strings.
To use the step a caller creates the context and initializes its data with an array that has at least one element.
After creating the context the caller writes its name into the data array under the Name key, which is why the caller and the step must agree on the key positions.
A data array of length one only works because the Name key happens to sit at position zero, so the caller must know that layout.
After creating the context the caller writes its name into the data array under the Name key, which is why the caller and the step must agree on the key positions.
To avoid depending on the literal index zero the caller can build an array with enough elements that the required position always exists.
Sizing the context array by the required positions rather than by one element is what keeps the key positions stable for the step.
The constructed context object can be passed directly to the step, and the step will work because it resolves data through the shared key constants.
A helper method is introduced so the caller code for building and filling the context is not duplicated, and it is reused for the Dog and Cockroach steps with only the name passed in.

A first drawback is that both the calling code and the executing code must use exactly the same constants, though sharing public constants already handles this.

The real drawback is that a context may carry many keys and different systems read different cells from it, so any positional scheme couples unrelated features together.
For example one system could use context A at index 2 and context B at index 3 while another system expects its own key at index 4.
A system that only needs its own key still has to allocate a context array long enough to cover every position up to it, wasting memory for cells it never reads.
Creating the context array allocates memory for every position up to that key, so the array has five cells although only one is ever used, which wastes memory.
Writing an int value into an object-typed slot boxes it and allocates extra memory, a smaller problem in this context than the type mismatches.
The most important problem is the casts and the requirement to write exactly the expected type into the context under a given key.

The first fix targets the array sizing so that only cells for keys that actually exist are allocated.
Casting the stored type into the type you need is the second fix for the context design.
The second fix requires casting the stored value to the type you actually need.
The boxing problem is deliberately left unfixed because it is usually ignored and not solved at the framework or fundamental level.
Boxing is handled above the framework with the flyweight pattern, a pool of reusable objects that hold the data instead of the values being boxed directly.
In game development the same boxing problem is solved with the ECS pattern.
In ECS each data type is stored in its own array, so all names go into one large array and all sums into another array for the whole context.
Callers pass an identifier instead of the arrays themselves and look the data up in the type-specific arrays, which keeps boxing out of the hot path.
The fourth and hardest problem of the context design is key collisions.
An unnoticed off-by-one mistake, for example writing key 0 instead of 1, crashes the program at runtime.
The crash happens because name data and number data were stored under the same key, and neither static analysis nor program startup reveals it.
Such a wrong-type conflict only surfaces when the expected-type context value is extracted, so the damage is deferred until that call.
Collisions are unlikely when a single shared key list is written by one author, since the same mistake is unlikely to be made twice.
Another module, such as a pipelines or dynamic-context module, has its own key list whose keys can conflict with yours.
Modules that share a context system can carry independent key lists, so your keys may collide with another module's keys.
Key conflicts are solved by using strings as keys or by routing all key assignment through a key registry instead of hardcoding key constants.
The registry hands out key values dynamically at runtime rather than having them written directly next to their use sites.
Because any other module using contexts also goes through the same registry, it can never receive the same keys that you received.
The cost of a key registry is that key assignment now depends on system initialization order: the module that runs first takes the lower keys and reversing the order swaps who gets which keys.
The lesson deliberately focuses only on the array-sizing and casting problems, since the array problem is fixed simply by using a dictionary and the casting problem follows from it.
The first problem with storing context data is easiest to solve by simply using a dictionary.
The second problem is solved simply with the typed-key pattern, which the instructor considers a very useful pattern to apply always.
With a typed key you do not store just an int under the key but also statically keep the type of what it points to in the variable, which is what makes the pattern useful.
The array of objects is replaced with a dictionary keyed by data so that less memory is used.
The dictionary can be created with capacity two because only two context elements are ever added to it.

Inside the context a dictionary holding a single element is created in place of the previous structure.

Dictionaries are the usual way to store such contexts, and libraries typically use strict keys to reduce key conflicts.
Beyond dictionaries other approaches exist and are only mentioned briefly in this lesson.
In the list alternative the objects are distinguished by their type rather than their position, so getting the sum means scanning the list to find the int.

Attaching the key to the value object itself, and storing lists of keys and values, is another valid way to resolve the ambiguity of an int key.
A further approach stores a list of components, and this pattern is used often in game development, for example in Unity.
The component-list approach is not the best option, since ECS is the better approach for game development, though the simpler approach is still widely used.
In this approach the component type is the key, the component holds a field for the sum, and the needed components are added to the list and later searched by type.
This variant is often optimized by using a dictionary of components that is looked up by type.
Even so, the plain key-value dictionary without extra machinery is applied far more often.

The context exposes methods for interacting with that hidden dictionary, and those methods are strictly typed.

Inside the context the keys can stay plain ints, but the user never touches them directly and instead uses an abstraction key object that carries the value field and the type information as a parameter.

The registry pattern centralizes key creation in one class, possibly static, that hands out fresh keys from a counter that starts at zero.
The registry exposes a generic static method NextKey<T> whose type parameter tells it which kind of key the caller needs.
NextKey<T> creates a key for the requested type and returns the newly created counter value, so callers never build key objects themselves.
The method stores the current counter value into a local variable and returns that value as the new key.
Only after returning does the registry increment its counter, so every subsequent call yields a different key.
A registry shared across several systems with static fields and static classes becomes global state, which is hard to reuse in other places.
The recommended shape is a non-static registry class accessed through the singleton pattern instead of a static class with static fields.
Ideally the singleton instance lives outside the class that consumes it so that it stays maximally extensible and the consumer does not depend on it structurally.
Because the key is nominally generic but only ever used inside one context, ideally that context would define its own key type and its own registry with methods specialized to that key type.
The instructor explicitly leaves the specialized per-context key type and registry unimplemented because it would take too much time.

In practice one generalized registry is usually enough, accepting some duplication for different key types while keeping most of the code shared and hiding the differences behind wrappers or static methods.
If stricter typing is wanted, an additional wrapper class with specialized methods for a concrete key type can be layered on top of the shared registry.
That extra wrapper is again mentioned but not implemented here, and the lesson keeps the simplified version.
A registry instance is introduced as a single instance named KeyRegistry, created once and used to hand out keys.
The registry class is static because it is only used from a static context once when the program starts to obtain that context's keys.
Being a singleton does not prevent the registry from also being used through a non-static reference.
Each key is obtained from the registry exactly once with a call like NextKey<string>, and the result is assigned to a field rather than read through a getter property.
The keys must live in fields, not be recomputed on each use, because every registry call would mint new keys while the stored values must stay bound to fixed keys.
Because keys now come from a counter instead of global uninitialized values, collisions between keys can no longer occur.

A remaining risk is a race condition if two threads request keys at the same moment, which would need atomic operations; the instructor leaves this for students to research, noting thread safety otherwise works fine.
If keys are registered through the registry in this way, the key store itself could equally be replaced by another data structure.
You can back the registry with a data structure that records which type each registered key holds, which is what makes introspection of stored values possible.
A method such as GetOfKey(key) can return the type stored for a given key, so callers can ask the registry what a key's value type is.
Even for a key that is unknown as a static member, you can still query its type as long as you know the number it is stored under.
A context method PrintCurrentData is added to dump the current registry contents while debugging.
PrintCurrentData walks the data in a loop and writes one console line per key stating that a value of a given type is stored under that key.
Persisting just the type of each value is not very useful in practice, so a better design is to attach richer information instead.
You can pass metadata when creating a key, for example the key's name, and keep those names in a separate list.
Key names are collected into their own list, for example keyNames, so the numeric key can be mapped back to a readable name.
PrintCurrentData holds a key and its value and calls GetName on the global registry to print that a value lives under that key's name.
Keeping metadata centrally in the registry rather than inside each key means the information is globally available and is never duplicated per key.
Names must be supplied at key creation time, so the demo prints what has been created in the context to confirm registration.
A call such as keys.AddName(name, key) is added to register the name of the key that was just created.
Even though the keys themselves are just integers held in memory, the registry can still produce names and type metadata for them.
PrintCurrentData queries the registry to learn what each integer key represents before printing it.
Many libraries take a simpler route than storing type metadata: they just keep strings or use the strings themselves as keys.
A registry keyed by strings only needs to check that no two keys share the same name, keeping a set of already existing names.
HashSet.Add returns true only when the value was not present before, so its return value is what signals whether the key name was new.
When Add reports the key was already present, the registry throws an exception saying the key already exists or is already registered.
In the string-keyed registry the key value is the name itself, so the int stored before the name registration is now replaced by the string name.
This variant stops keeping metadata altogether and stores values under string keys instead of under numeric ones.
Storing by key is slower than storing by index because indexed lookups skip hash computation while string keys require a hash to be calculated.
The payoff is easier conflict handling: a library can simply declare that it owns a namespaced key, so collisions should never happen.
If you skip the registry and create string keys yourself, collisions become a real problem the registry could otherwise have caught.
The weakness of string keys is that nothing stops you from passing or creating a key the registry never issued, such as your own string key.
A key object can be constructed by client code itself instead of being obtained from the key registry, which bypasses the registration mechanism.
Hand-creating a key with the same string value as an existing one and lying to the compiler about the type crashes at runtime because the registry actually stored an int under that name.
Keys can be made creatable only by the registry by making the key constructor internal, saving the value into a field and removing the public constructor.

The code still compiles after making the constructor internal only because the library and the program live in the same project, and from a separate imported library the internal constructor would be unusable.
If the code were in another library that merely imported this one, calling the internal constructor would be a compilation error.
Nobody is likely to create keys manually this way because the user would also have to know the actual key type the registry stored.
Restricting key creation to the registry is only a minimal, entirely optional protection, not a required measure.
